  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Car Similarity: Similar cars
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Vignette:
The intersection on Route 9 still occupies the space where Samir used to picture his future. It had been a straightforward commute, rain slicking the asphalt, when a delivery van ran a red light and clipped his sedan at forty miles per hour. The impact had been a concussive roar, followed by the sharp hiss of a ruptured radiator and the sudden, heavy scent of spilled liquor from a cooler in the van’s cab. Glass rained across his lap. He remembers the steering column buckling inward, the tires screeching, the metallic groan of crumpled steel wrapping around his door. For weeks after, the smell of bourbon and cheap whiskey clung to him, a ghost of that cooler’s contents that he caught whenever a taxi idled too close to his building or a colleague’s lunch contained a strong spirit. He began to see the wrecked cars not as unfortunate incidents but as immediate threats, each crumpled hood and shattered windshield pulling him back to the exact angle of impact, especially the identical make and model he had been driving that evening. In the months that followed, Samir found his body locked in a state of perpetual readiness. He was certain that another collision was always one misjudged turn away, and he watched the road with a narrow, unblinking focus that left him exhausted by noon. Ordinary noises became detonations; the office printer jamming, a heavy briefcase dropped in the hallway, even the microwave beep in the breakroom sent him jolting out of his seat, heart hammering against his ribs. He could not explain why he felt so exposed, only that the world had turned sharp and unpredictable. As the days stretched, a quiet conviction took root: he could no longer trust his own instincts behind the wheel, or anywhere else. The precision that had defined his work as a tax inspector—meticulous audits, careful calculations, the steady rhythm of field visits—felt suddenly out of reach. He was no longer capable of doing the things that had built his reputation, and he feared he would never again feel the steady baseline of normal emotion, as if something vital had been sheared away in that intersection. Samir’s days took on a rigid architecture. He parked his car in a municipal garage he now avoided entirely, switching to public transit where sudden bus brakes sent his shoulders tightening against his spine. The thought of driving or riding as a passenger felt insurmountable, so he requested a transfer to remote case review, quietly stepping away from the field audits that once occupied his weeks. Alongside these adjustments, he found himself spending long hours on his phone, losing entire evenings to strategy games and endless scrolling, or simply skipping meals until the hunger pains dulled into a familiar static. His ex-wife, Layla, had not waited for the slow withdrawal to resolve; their divorce papers were signed months earlier, and their separation stood as another quiet fact of his rearranged life. The undereating left him dizzy during case meetings, and the screen escape no longer quieted the static in his head. Now at thirty, Samir sits in a clinician’s office with a cup of water he barely drinks. He came because the paralysis of avoidance has begun to bleed into his sleep, because the hypervigilance has made the office environment feel unmanageable, and because he can no longer outrun the memory of the crushed metal. He is most afraid that he has permanently fractured his capacity to function, that the man who once navigated complex fiscal investigations with confidence is gone, replaced by someone who jumps at a dropped pen and trusts nothing, least of all himself. What he hopes for, quietly and desperately, is to remember what it feels like to move through the world without bracing for impact, to trust his own mind again, and to stop counting the exits.
